questions.question: What is a pull request (PR) and why is it used?
questions.title: What Is a Pull Request?
questions.direct_answer: A pull request is a mechanism on hosting platforms like GitHub or GitLab to propose merging a feature branch into another branch, enabling code review, discussion, and automated checks before the merge happens. It's the gatekeeping step that ensures code quality and team alignment before changes reach production.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of professional team collaboration workflows — PRs are the gatekeeping mechanism for production code quality and team alignment.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Describing a PR purely as a technical merge operation without mentioning the human review process, discussion, and quality gates.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that PR descriptions and linked issues become part of the project's documentation and audit trail, helping future developers understand why decisions were made.

sections.title: What is a Pull Request and Why Teams Use It
sections.content: A **pull request** (PR) is a workflow feature provided by Git hosting platforms like GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket that sits between your feature branch and the main codebase. Think of it as a quality gate at a factory — your code can't enter production until it passes inspection. When you open a PR, you're saying "here's my work, please review it before merging." The PR becomes a discussion thread where teammates can comment on specific lines, suggest changes, approve or request modifications, and see automated test results. This process catches bugs early, spreads knowledge across the team (reviewers learn from your code), and maintains a **clean main branch** that always works. The PR itself — with its description, comments, and linked issues — becomes **permanent documentation** explaining not just what changed, but why those changes were necessary. Without PRs, teams would merge untested code directly, creating chaos in production.

sections.title: Typical Pull Request Workflow in a Spring Boot Project
Key Points
content: **Code review gate**: PRs require human approval before merging, catching bugs and design issues early before production.
**Discussion thread**: Each PR has comments, replies, and inline code annotations — the team discusses trade-offs in context.
**Automated checks**: CI pipelines run tests, linting, and security scans automatically when you open a PR — failures block the merge.
**Audit trail**: PR history shows who approved what changes and when, critical for compliance and understanding past decisions.
**Knowledge sharing**: Reviewing others' PRs teaches you patterns and libraries used across the codebase — it's how juniors learn.
**Branch protection**: Teams configure rules like "require 2 approvals" or "all tests must pass" — the platform enforces quality standards.
**Issue linkage**: PRs typically reference Jira tickets or GitHub issues, connecting code changes to business requirements.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A pull request is the standard way teams review and merge code changes before they hit production. When I finish a feature on a branch, I open a PR to propose merging it into main. The PR isn't just a merge — it's a discussion. My teammates can see the code diff, leave comments on specific lines, and ask questions. Meanwhile, automated tests run to catch bugs I might've missed. For example, if I added validation logic to an order service, the PR shows exactly what changed and why. My tech lead reviews it, maybe suggests renaming a variable for clarity, and once they approve and tests pass, I can merge. The cool part is that the entire conversation — the description, comments, approvals — stays in the PR history forever. Six months later, if someone wonders why we validate quantity, they can find that PR and read the discussion. One common mistake freshers make is opening a PR without explaining anything in the description. That forces the reviewer to guess your intent, which slows everything down. Always write a clear description linking to the related issue. That's what makes code review efficient and keeps the team moving fast.

questions.question: What are the different merge strategies available when merging a pull request on GitHub?
questions.title: PR Merge Strategies: Merge, Squash, Rebase
questions.direct_answer: GitHub offers three merge strategies: Merge commit (creates a merge commit preserving all branch history), Squash and merge (combines all PR commits into a single commit with a clean message), and Rebase and merge (replays commits linearly without creating a merge commit). Each has different trade-offs for history readability and auditability.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical workflow knowledge — this comes up in daily work discussions and team code review practices where strategy choice affects repository history.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only knowing the basic merge exists — not realizing squash is the most popular choice for keeping main branch history clean and readable.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain which strategy suits which team philosophy — squash for clean main, rebase for linear history purists, merge commit for full auditability and traceability.

sections.title: Understanding GitHub's Three Merge Strategies
sections.content: When you're ready to merge a pull request, GitHub gives you three options that change how your branch commits appear in the **main branch history**. This isn't just a technical detail — it affects how readable your Git log is and how easy it is to understand what changed when. **Merge commit** creates a new commit that ties together your branch and main, keeping every individual commit from your feature branch visible. **Squash and merge** takes all your messy work-in-progress commits ("fix typo," "oops forgot semicolon") and combines them into one clean commit with a good message. **Rebase and merge** replays your commits one by one on top of main, creating a linear history without merge commits. Teams pick one as their standard based on whether they value detailed audit trails or clean, readable history. Most modern teams prefer squash because main stays clean while the full detail remains in the PR itself.

sections.title: How Each Strategy Affects Git History
Key Points
content: **Merge commit**: Creates a merge commit with two parents, preserving the entire branch structure and every individual commit in the feature branch.
**Squash and merge**: Condenses all PR commits into one new commit on main, ideal for keeping main history clean and readable — most popular choice.
**Rebase and merge**: Takes each commit from the PR and replays it on main without a merge commit, creating a linear history — purist's choice.
**Main history impact**: Squash gives you one line per feature in git log, merge shows every work-in-progress commit, rebase shows commits but no merge bubbles.
**Revert complexity**: Squashed commits are easiest to revert (one commit), merge commits revert the whole branch cleanly, rebased commits must be reverted individually.
**Team standard**: Most teams pick one strategy and enforce it via branch protection rules — consistency matters more than which you choose.
**PR preservation**: The full commit-by-commit detail always remains visible in the closed PR regardless of merge strategy, so nothing is truly lost.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: GitHub gives you three ways to merge a pull request, and they each affect your main branch history differently. Merge commit is the traditional approach — it creates a merge commit that shows your feature branch merging into main, keeping all your individual commits visible. If you made ten commits on your branch, all ten show up in main's history. That's great for auditability but can make git log messy. Squash and merge is the most popular choice these days. It takes all your commits — including the ones like fix typo or oops — and combines them into one clean commit with a good message. So your feature shows as one line in main's history, but the detailed commit-by-commit work is still visible in the PR itself. Rebase and merge is the purist option. It replays your commits one by one on top of main without creating a merge commit, giving you a perfectly linear history. It looks clean but loses the visual grouping of which commits belonged to which feature. Most teams I've seen use squash by default because it keeps main readable. One mistake freshers make is not realizing these strategies are configurable per-repo. Ask your team lead which one they use. If you merge the wrong way, it's annoying to fix.

questions.question: What should you include in a pull request to make it easy to review?
questions.title: Pull Request Best Practices
questions.direct_answer: A good pull request includes a clear description explaining what changed and why, a linked issue or ticket number, a focused scope with minimal unrelated changes, passing automated tests, and relevant screenshots or examples. The goal is to make the reviewer's job as easy as possible, enabling fast, thorough review.

interviewer_intent.testing: Professional habits and empathy for reviewers — shows the candidate understands team dynamics and respects others' time during code review.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Opening a 2000-line PR with no description or mixing multiple unrelated features — this is a common junior habit that frustrates teams and delays reviews.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention self-reviewing your own PR before requesting review — catching your own typos, formatting issues, and obvious bugs first shows maturity and professionalism.

sections.title: What Makes a Pull Request Easy to Review
sections.content: Writing a good pull request is an act of **empathy** — you're making your reviewer's job easier, which means faster approval and less back-and-forth. A great PR tells a clear story: here's the problem, here's what I changed, here's why I made these choices, and here's how to verify it works. Start with a **descriptive title** that summarizes the change ("Add email validation to user registration" not "fix stuff"). The description should link to the Jira ticket or GitHub issue, explain the approach you took, and call out anything tricky or unusual. Keep the scope **small and focused** — ideally under 400 lines of changes. If you fixed a bug and also refactored three classes, split that into two PRs. Include **screenshots** for UI changes or **example API responses** for backend endpoints. Make sure tests pass before requesting review. Finally, do a **self-review** first — read through your own diff, catch formatting issues, remove debug prints, and comment on complex sections yourself. Reviewers notice when you've done this prep work, and it builds trust.

sections.title: Example of a Well-Structured Pull Request
Key Points
content: **Clear description**: Explain the problem being solved, your approach, and any trade-offs — don't make the reviewer guess your intent.
**Linked issue**: Reference the Jira ticket or GitHub issue so reviewers understand the business context and acceptance criteria.
**Small scope**: Keep PRs under 400 lines when possible — large PRs get rubber-stamped without real review, defeating the purpose.
**Passing tests**: Ensure CI is green before requesting review — asking someone to review broken code wastes their time.
**Visual aids**: Include screenshots for UI changes, example JSON for API endpoints, or logs showing the fix working — make verification easy.
**Self-review first**: Read through your own diff before submitting, catching typos, console logs, and commented-out code yourself.
**Highlight complexity**: Add comments in the PR itself explaining tricky logic or unusual patterns — guide the reviewer to what matters most.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A good pull request makes the reviewer's life easy. That means being clear about what changed and why. First, write a descriptive title — something like Add email validation to user signup, not just Fix bug. In the description, link to the Jira ticket so the reviewer knows the business context. Then explain your approach. If you added validation logic, say where you put it and why. Call out any trade-offs, like I used IllegalArgumentException here instead of a custom exception to keep it simple. Keep the PR focused. If you're fixing a bug, don't also refactor unrelated code. That makes review harder because the reviewer has to think about two things at once. For backend changes, include example requests and responses. For frontend changes, add screenshots. Make sure all tests pass before you hit request review — green CI is non-negotiable. Here's the thing most freshers miss: self-review your own PR first. Open the files changed tab and read through your diff like you're the reviewer. You'll catch your own typos, leftover debug statements, and formatting issues. When reviewers see you've done that prep work, they trust you more and review faster. A sloppy PR with no description signals you don't respect their time. A polished PR with clear explanations signals you're a professional.

questions.question: What is a draft pull request and when would you use it?
questions.title: Draft Pull Requests
questions.direct_answer: A draft pull request signals that the work is still in progress and not ready for formal review — it enables early feedback, visibility to the team, and CI checks without requesting a full review. Teams use it to get architectural input before investing heavily in implementation details.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of collaboration features and good team communication habits that prevent wasted work on wrong approaches.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing draft PRs exist and instead opening a regular PR with a title like WIP: don't merge yet, which clutters the review queue.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that draft PRs are great for getting early architectural feedback before investing in a full implementation — asking is this the right approach saves rework.

sections.title: When and Why to Use Draft Pull Requests
sections.content: A **draft pull request** is GitHub's built-in way to say "I'm working on this, but it's not ready for formal review yet." When you mark a PR as draft, it signals to your team that you're still iterating — don't spend time reviewing every line yet. Draft PRs are perfect for three scenarios: getting **early architectural feedback** ("am I solving this the right way?"), making your work **visible to the team** so they know what you're building, and triggering **CI checks** to catch integration issues early. For example, if you're adding a new REST endpoint but unsure whether to use a DTO or return the entity directly, open a draft PR and ask your tech lead for input. That five-minute conversation can save hours of rework. Draft PRs also prevent the awkward situation where someone else starts building the same feature because they didn't know you were working on it. When your code is ready, you click "Ready for review" and the PR transitions to normal review mode. It's a small feature that prevents big communication problems.

sections.title: Step 1: Use Draft PRs for Early Architectural Feedback
sections.content: The most valuable use of a draft PR is asking for direction **before** you've built everything. Let's say you're implementing a caching layer for a service. You write the basic structure — maybe a CacheService interface and a Redis implementation — but you're unsure if you should use Spring's at-Cacheable annotation or manually manage cache keys. Open a draft PR with just that skeleton code and tag your tech lead: "Hey, I'm planning to add caching here. Does this approach look right, or should I use Spring's built-in annotations instead?" If they steer you toward annotations, you've saved yourself from building a custom implementation that would've been thrown away. This is especially important for freshers — you don't have ten years of experience to know all the patterns. Asking early shows humility and prevents wasted effort. The key is framing it as "Is this the right direction?" not "Review every line."

sections.title: Step 2: Use Draft PRs for Team Visibility and CI Validation
sections.content: Even if you don't need architectural feedback, draft PRs make your work visible to the team. If you're building a big feature over several days, opening a draft PR on day one means your teammates can see the branch exists and what you're working on. This prevents duplicate work — someone won't start building the same thing because they didn't know you were on it. Draft PRs also trigger **continuous integration checks** immediately. Your tests run, linters check formatting, security scans look for vulnerabilities. If your branch breaks the build or has a dependency conflict with main, you find out now, not three days later when you're ready to merge. Some teams even require draft PRs for any work that'll take more than a day, just to keep everyone in sync. When you're done, you mark it "Ready for review" and the real review process starts. Think of draft status as a temporary shield that says please don't review yet but feel free to look and give input.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Draft status**: Marks a PR as work-in-progress — reviewers know not to do a full line-by-line review yet, just high-level feedback.
**Early feedback**: Best use case is getting architectural direction before investing heavily in implementation details that might need rework.
**Team visibility**: Makes your work visible on the PR board so teammates know what you're building and won't duplicate effort.
**CI checks run**: Draft PRs trigger automated tests, linting, and security scans — you catch integration issues early before final review.
**Ready for review transition**: When you're done, click the button to convert draft to normal PR — it enters the review queue officially.
**Avoids WIP titles**: Using draft status is cleaner than opening a regular PR with a title like WIP: don't merge, which clutters the review list.
**Prevents wasted work**: Asking is this the right approach in a draft PR saves hours of building something that gets rejected in review later.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: A draft pull request is GitHub's way of saying this isn't ready for review yet. When you mark a PR as draft, it tells your team you're still working on it and they shouldn't spend time doing a full review. The biggest value is getting early feedback before you've invested too much time. For example, let's say I'm adding a new caching layer to a service. I write the basic structure — maybe a CacheService interface and a simple implementation — but I'm not sure if I should use Spring's at-Cacheable annotation or roll my own solution. I'll open a draft PR and tag my tech lead with a question: Does this approach look right? If they say use the annotation, I've just saved myself hours of building a custom solution that would've been rejected anyway. Draft PRs also make your work visible to the team. If I'm building a feature that'll take three days, opening a draft on day one means no one else will start the same work. And here's a practical benefit: draft PRs trigger CI checks. My tests run, linters check my code, and I find out immediately if I broke something or have a merge conflict. When I'm done, I click ready for review and it becomes a normal PR. One mistake freshers make is opening a regular PR with a title like WIP don't merge. That's messy. Just use the draft feature. It's cleaner and signals intent clearly.

questions.question: How do you address review comments on a pull request?
questions.title: Addressing Pull Request Review Comments
questions.direct_answer: Address review comments by making the requested code changes, committing them to the same branch, which automatically updates the PR — then respond to each comment explaining what you changed or why you respectfully disagree. Clear communication in the comment thread keeps the review moving and shows professionalism.

interviewer_intent.testing: Communication skills and professional collaboration etiquette during code review — how candidates handle feedback reveals maturity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Ignoring comments or just pushing changes without explaining what was done — leaving the reviewer to re-read everything and guess what changed.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that code review is a conversation, not a verdict — it's okay to respectfully disagree and discuss trade-offs if you have good reasoning.

sections.title: How to Handle Code Review Comments Professionally
sections.content: Addressing review comments is where **collaboration skills** matter as much as coding skills. When a reviewer leaves feedback, they're investing their time to help you improve — treat their comments as valuable input, not criticism. The mechanical part is simple: make the code changes they suggested, commit to your feature branch, and push. The PR updates automatically with your new commits. The communication part is where freshers often fail: **respond to each comment** explaining what you did. If they said "extract this into a method," reply with "Done, created validateOrderQuantity method in commit abc123." This closes the feedback loop so the reviewer knows you addressed it without re-reading everything. If you **disagree** with a suggestion, that's okay — explain your reasoning politely. Maybe they suggested a pattern that doesn't fit your use case. Reply with something like "I see your point, but I kept the current approach because X. Happy to discuss if you feel strongly." Code review is a **conversation**, not a one-way command. The goal is producing the best code together, not blindly following orders.

sections.title: Example of Responding to Review Comments
Key Points
content: **Make changes on same branch**: Commit fixes to your feature branch and push — the PR updates automatically, no need to open a new PR.
**Respond to each comment**: Reply explaining what you changed or why you kept it as-is — close the feedback loop so reviewers know you addressed their input.
**Reference commit hashes**: When saying you fixed something, link to the commit or line number so the reviewer can verify easily without searching.
**Resolve vs reply**: Use GitHub's resolve conversation button only after both you and the reviewer agree the issue is addressed — don't resolve unilaterally.
**Disagree respectfully**: If you think a suggestion doesn't apply, explain your reasoning politely — code review is a discussion, not orders from above.
**Batch responses**: If you have ten comments, address them all in one commit and one reply round rather than ping-ponging with ten separate commits.
**Thank reviewers**: A simple thanks for the feedback shows appreciation — reviews take time and effort, acknowledge that contribution.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: When a reviewer leaves comments on my pull request, I treat it as a conversation, not a list of commands. First, I read through all the comments to understand the full picture — sometimes one comment affects another. Then I make the code changes they suggested. I commit those changes to my feature branch and push, which automatically updates the PR. Here's the key part freshers often miss: I respond to each comment explaining what I did. If they said extract this into a method, I reply with something like Done, created validateOrderQuantity method in commit abc1234. That way the reviewer knows I addressed it without having to re-read the entire diff. If I disagree with a suggestion, I don't just ignore it. I explain why. For example, maybe they suggested using a library, but that library pulls in ten dependencies for one method we need. I'd reply politely: I see your point, but I kept the manual implementation to avoid the dependency bloat. Happy to discuss if you feel strongly. Code review is about finding the best solution together, not just doing what you're told. One mistake I see juniors make is pushing changes without commenting, leaving the reviewer to guess what changed. That's frustrating and slows down the review. Another mistake is resolving comment threads yourself before the reviewer agrees. Use the resolve button only after both of you agree it's addressed. Finally, always thank your reviewer. They spent their time helping you improve. A simple thanks for the feedback goes a long way.
